note: full-refactor-of-enemies-and-combat pass 3, and the first sighting where the flake landed on the clause it would have decided. c18 IS 'merge-ready passes', so a red npm test leg inside merge-ready is not a nuisance here, it is the verdict. The first merge-ready run at head 9f49923 reported 'npm test FAIL exit=1' with no test named; a standalone 'npm test -- --reporter=dot' immediately after passed 81 files and 2161 tests in 42s, and a second full merge-ready then passed every leg including npm test. Cost roughly nine minutes of re-running, and the decision it forced is the real cost: an auditor cannot tell a flake from a regression from merge-ready's output, which names neither the test nor the file, so the honest options are to grade c18 unmet on one red run or to re-run until it agrees - and re-running until it agrees is exactly the habit this record says teaches everyone to wave a real regression through.

head: 9f49923bf9a2dd1f82c6e90ee093083b7b171301
note: full-refactor-of-enemies-and-combat pass 3, same prefix-classification rule, third distinct shape on this one spec. Two refused filings. The first: the deferral reason still has no flag - the generated pass file and AUDIT_USAGE both say deferred is 'refused with no reason', so I wrote '--reason 12=...' and it refused with 'error: --reason describes a finding, and no --finding has been opened yet'. The reason belongs in --evidence N=, which nothing says. The second: one continuation line inside clause 17's evidence was a git pathspec, '-- src/grammar/condition.ts ...' at column zero, and it refused with 'error: -- describes a finding, and no --finding has been opened yet' - the token it names is the bare separator, so the message reads as nonsense until you grep the file for ^-- and diff against the flag set, which is exactly the recovery the 2026-08-08 occurrence describes. An auditor whose evidence quotes a git command is the ordinary case, not an edge one, and the fix is unchanged: name the line and the file, say which shape was expected, and give the deferral reason a flag or say in the template that it goes in --evidence.

Thorns is 'on struck them:' on the carrier, not 'a persistent effect on damage-taken'; poison authored as a passive is 'on hit them:' on the entity rather than on the weapon's action, and 'on hit self:' is now 'on hit me:'. The four fixtures are all still expressible and this record's own preference for carrying them on the actor is now the cheaper form, not the harder one. head: 86a4096ec7eff3a6739e6677f93e4b916c710413
note: combat-events' actor-carried primitive is a hook block on the entity, not a handler on a '# event'. The event vocabulary it was written to consume never arrived - skill-levels-xp-events shipped the curve only and left the closed set to xp-from-events - and the one that did arrive binds a name to a pool crossing a threshold, which a landed swing is not. Reaching thorns through '# event' would have cost four changes to shipped mechanisms: new triggers that are not threshold crossings, a collision with xp-from-events' eight, a widening of credit: from causer to other-party, and a resource: field on an event that has no pool. 'on struck them:' on the carrier costs none of them. This overturns the recorded decision that a persistent effect names one event from a vocabulary, and reverses the conclusion - not the reasoning - of the decision that dropped 'when hit:', whose argument was against an action-declared pair and does not reach an entity-declared one.

head: 6ec7010fbbb2986a305fc393c9e90f6d38e53cf8
note: combat-events is corrected 2026-08-09: an '# action' is not a carrier of effects. The first re-plan's four hook block names hung off the action host and the sword refutes it - equipping a blade that poisons cannot mean the wearer performs a different attack, and with one shared melee-combat a hook on the action fires for every entity that swings. A hook is a character modifier, carried by an '# entity' block or an equipped '# item' and gathered by the same walk statRange folds a stat bonus from, so a passive and a buff join as carriers without a second mechanism. That collapses four block names to two verbs read from the carrier - 'on hit:' and 'when hit:' - with 'them:' as the one marked redirect, and it dissolves stat-bonus-per-counter as a separate slice, since a counter-scaled bonus and a hook are the same job over the same fold. Overturns the recorded decision that action-declared and actor-carried hooks both survive because their scopes differ: the scope it defended is not one the game wants.

head: 6ec7010fbbb2986a305fc393c9e90f6d38e53cf8
note: credit: is renamed them: by combat-events rather than left as a filed question. Under the corrected design a hook's results default to the carrying character and one wrapper redirects them to the other party the moment identifies - the struck party under 'on hit:', the swinger under 'when hit:', the killer in an 'on death:' handler. credit: already is that wrapper for the third case alone and its name states an intent rather than a side, which reads as the opposite of what happens when the results are poison or thorns. The rename closes credit-names-an-intent-where-the-grammar-elsewhere-names-a-s, costs one case in effects.ts, one emitter in serialize.ts and four test fixtures, and touches no shipped content.

head: 6ec7010fbbb2986a305fc393c9e90f6d38e53cf8

head: 6ec7010fbbb2986a305fc393c9e90f6d38e53cf8
note: The 2026-08-09 note against this record is superseded the same day. Hooks are not entity-declared blocks named on hit them:/on struck me:; they are character modifiers carried by an # entity block, an equipped # item or (yours) a # passive, and there are two of them: 'on hit:' and 'when hit:', both read from the character carrying them, with 'them:' redirecting results to the other party. So thorns is 'when hit: them: drain: N health' on a passive, poison is 'on hit: them: <debuff>', rage is 'on hit: restore: 1 rage' beside '+N attack per rage' on the same passive, and none of the four needs an action of its own. This is closer to how you already author a passive than the shape either earlier draft had.

A prefix form on the pool name - 'drain: 3 their health', matching 'depletes: their health' - was considered and lost: it reaches only results that name a pool, so xp:, give: and roll: would keep the wrapper and the language would carry two spellings of one idea.

note: combat-hook-grammar: the two hook labels are claimed as SECTION FIELDS on # entity and # item rather than as a third shape for entityBlock's label dispatch, which is what the task's deliverable forecast. A hook is a fixed-name result block, which is what 'on success:' / 'on failure:' / 'on unfinished:' already are one level down, and spelling it as a field buys the once-guard, the typo hint, the inline-or-block reader and '+on hit:' append from machinery that exists. It also puts the label ahead of the handler dispatch by construction: 'on hit:' cannot be read as a handler for an event named 'hit' because the field table is consulted first. The cost the forecast was pricing - an item restructured so its labelled blocks are no longer all actions - is not paid: item.actions still holds only actions.

I aimed the tool's own path for the first manifest and used the step-0 prefix for the second and for every probe fixture, so the run now spans two naming schemes and a reader cannot tell which files are mine. The success line - 'recorded pass 1 ... 8 finding(s) recorded' - is printed FIRST and is then followed by roughly 200 lines of prior-art and rulings dumps, one block per file the findings name. I read the tail, saw only prior art, and re-ran the identical command to see what it had said; that appended pass 2 with standings identical to pass 1 and eight duplicate findings, combat-events-pass2-* beside combat-events-pass1-*. Recovery was eight  invocations, about four minutes, and the spec now carries a second recorded pass that measured nothing. Two cheap fixes, either sufficient: refuse a second pass at the same head unless told to, or repeat the outcome line after the prior-art dump so a tail sees it.

head: e90fd17d1f0966be7af6ddcecac83de2021c2a54
note: Open question 3 answered: the recorder follows the commands down. /create-test emits directive text, which is the recorded spelling of what the commands did, so it cannot live above the module that decides that spelling. The driver holds no recorder logic; it hands its Recorder to newContext and never touches history.

head: e90fd17d1f0966be7af6ddcecac83de2021c2a54
note: A slash line is looked up by its leading token, not by string prefix, so /create-valid-test no longer has to be tested before /create-test and adding a command cannot shadow one. It tightens three inputs that used to be accepted: /wait30, /loadfoo and /speedxyz reported their argument before and report 'unknown command' now. Deliberate, and no shipped # test or scripted transcript types any of them.

head: e90fd17d1f0966be7af6ddcecac83de2021c2a54
note: /help prints the table's entries and then this driver's three startup-argv lines. An argv line is not a command -- a second driver has no argv and prints none of them -- so it is not a second copy of the command set, and c2's property holds: a command added to COMMANDS is documented by that edit alone.

note: in-process-module-api pass 5, the occurrence the record was filed from, measured from the auditor's side. The brief opened with the WARNING that none of the clauses' work is in the diff, step 4 said 'no manifest was written' and step 7 said 'Do not file a pass' — while the branch's own in-progress member carries spec: in-process-module-api and discharges c1, c2, c3, c5, c6 and c8, and merge-ready's spec leg blocks on that member being open. An auditor who followed the printed brief would have graded nothing and filed nothing on the one branch these six clauses were finally built on. Cost: the whole verdict had to be authorised out of band by the commissioning message, and I hand-wrote both the args file and the 13-entry mutation manifest at paths the tool would otherwise have created.

head: 640445db6289d7d3c855a3075093df2360259d15
note: in-process-module-api pass 5. Fifth occurrence, and the fourth of five passes on this spec whose c8 is a before-and-after comparison with no supported way to get a base tree. I was explicitly forbidden to create a worktree (the pass-4 occurrence records why), so I found a cheaper substitute worth writing down: git show <base>:scripts/play-cli.ts back into the tree as scripts/zz-audit-base-cli.ts, beside the unchanged src/. Its relative imports resolve against the same repo root, node_modules is already there, the isEntryPoint guard keeps main() from running on import, and both drivers can then be loaded into ONE npm run inspect process and diffed against each other. It is exact only when the diff adds no file below the one being replaced — true here, since this branch's only new src file is command.ts — so it is not the general answer, but it cost two tool calls against the pass-4 auditor's four-plus-a-reinstall, and it is what let me take the base-vs-head transcript pass 4 declined to take. Cleanup is rm, not a recursive delete through a junction.

head: 640445db6289d7d3c855a3075093df2360259d15
note: in-process-module-api pass 5, the zero-generation half again and the sixth consecutive pass on this spec to pay it: all eight clauses are prose with no proof: target, and this time the brief did not even print the 'none' line — it printed 'No mutation manifest: the diff above is not in-process-module-api's', which is wrong on its face (see audit-prompt-refuses-to-write-a-pass-file...). Hand-built a 13-entry manifest after reading command.ts and play-cli.ts cold, aimed at the dispatch lookup, helpEntries, the tone/glyph boundary, the speed argument, and the three live-clock decision lines. 11 killed, 2 survived, and both survivors are findings this pass would not otherwise have: end()'s elapsed subtraction, which every existing test masks by starting at sim-time 0, and LiveProgress.implicit's !targeted guard, which the driver's own precedence masks. Neither line is reachable by a per-test expansion — no test file names either one. About 30 minutes. Also worth noting for the record's deliverable: the previous four passes' manifests are named in the spec's prose but only pass 3's and 4's files survived on disk in the shared temp directory, and neither was aimed at this branch's files, so nothing could be copied forward this time.

head: 640445db6289d7d3c855a3075093df2360259d15
note: in-process-module-api pass 5. Same shape, smaller blast radius, and the residual is now visible in isolation: this branch's member discharges c1, c2, c3, c5, c6 and c8, so I graded those six myself and only c7 is somebody else's — it is owed by layer-check-reads-every-source-file, which is open and named as its owner in the spec's own standings. Grading c7 unmet, which is the only honest grade since I checked it and it fails, minted in-process-module-api-clause-7-pass-5 as a fresh open undelivered record against this branch, duplicating an obligation that already has an owner and a record. The clause-8-pass-5 record is legitimate — c8 is this branch's and it fails. So the rule the deliverable states is exactly right and the discriminator is available in the store: file no undelivered record for a clause an open member of the same spec already owes.

New cost this time, which is why it is worth an occurrence rather than a shrug: the flake also destroyed a mutation verdict. npm run mutate escalated one c4 entry to whole-suite scope, scripts/tasks/handoff.test.ts failed there and did not reproduce, and the run returned UNSTABLE -- so the tool answered nothing about the line I aimed at, and I had to read the escalation chain by hand to recover the file-scope answer it had already measured. note: gui-rebuild pass 1, 2026-08-10: the zero-generation half again, on a UI spec this time. All ten clauses are prose with no proof: target, so step 4 printed 'no manifest was written' and 'none - no proof target on this spec resolved to a test this brief could name', and the brief added '10 of 10 clause(s) have no proof target and require human verification'. That last line is the sharpest version of the cost this record has recorded: five of the ten clauses are discharged by named vitest tests sitting in the same diff (surface.test.ts, render.test.tsx, driver.test.ts, shippedContent.test.ts, transient.test.ts), and the brief still classified every one of them as needing a human to look at the behaviour. Neither is reachable by a per-test generator: the first is a line I had to WRITE (a dynamic import that does not exist in the tree) rather than one to break, and the second is a JSX ternary no test file names.

head: 0b6774ea0080d9ce07f84b9ee68957471c24a783
note: The UI half of this cannot hold the clause on its own. A driver can only answer with a value the engine published, so an option with values: [] leaves no answer for any driver to render — the REPL is equally stuck, printing the label with no numbered line under it and refusing a typed submit-modal against optionRefusal. The seam is where the frame is made: src/runtime/session.ts applyDirective 'talk' opens a dialogueFrame for any non-null cursor, and src/runtime/dialogue-runtime.ts offered() can filter that cursor's menu down to nothing. Fixing it in src/ui would mean inventing an answer the engine never offered. CLAUDE.md's rule — enforce where a value is assembled, not where it is written — puts it in the Runtime system, and the behaviour it settles (a dialogue whose every choice is gated off ends rather than pauses) is a design decision the dialogue system owns, not the shell.

note: gui-rebuild c5: a run owns the GUI's session while it lasts. The driver drops a dispatch arriving mid-run and the sheet offers only the stop control, which is the REPL's paused readline rather than a command filter -- no command is refused, the moment is. The stop control is a glyph because a word for it would be prose no engine value published, the same reason the modal's submit is one. The driver logs the view each tick hands back, because a completion's say rides on that view and is drained from every view after it.

head: ac95fd0851ffddcd4337f8cd2000cdbf24f5d944
note: gui-rebuild c5: LIVE_TICK_MS moves from scripts/play-cli.ts to src/runtime/command.ts, beside LiveRun. Each tick rounds its own span through secondsToMs, so two drivers ticking at different cadences reach different states over one wall-clock span; the clause's 'same elapsed span' only means the same run if both read one figure. That is what widened the grant past src/ui.

head: 7726afa741da6cbb908f0a175182df2e33dfbdd8
note: gui-rebuild c5, overturning the earlier ruling on this record that a run owns the session while it lasts: the author's design is several actions at once, so a run does not withdraw the world's choices. It draws above them, outside the scroller, and until concurrency exists a dispatch replaces the run under way -- close(true) then runLine, so the spent time stands and nothing resolves against a world the next tick was about to move. Uniform over every dispatch rather than special-cased to a choice, because a driver that read the spelling of a line would be defining commands of its own.

head: 7726afa741da6cbb908f0a175182df2e33dfbdd8

The author read 200ms as visible steps in the progress bars; the bars now ease linearly over exactly one tick, so a fill arrives as the next tick leaves. Both drivers move together because the figure is shared -- play-cli's bar redraws twice as often too, which is the point of hoisting it.

note: Multi-leg travel routes only through places the player has already found, and may end in one they have not: stepping into the unknown is how a neighbour is discovered, and routing through the unknown would make the shape of the unfound map readable off a journey, which publishDiscovered already refuses to give away. The route is breadth-first over open edges, so it is the fewest legs and not the shortest walk -- distance is what a leg costs, not what picks one.

head: cee39aa21757eb7a6391fe8ffab4dc9519e6b051
note: SAVE_VERSION is not bumped for the journey field. The save is a sparse diff against initialState and loadSave clears what a save does not carry, so a save written before this branch loads with no walk under way, which is what it meant. A bump would invalidate every hand-written # save fixture to say nothing.

head: 13374c4d97573c9f2d348a6443ac81641cb87d14
note: gui-rebuild pass 6: asked it twice, and the second time it found the pass's main result. (1) Six tests in src/runtime/journey.test.ts were rewritten by the same commit that changed reachable(), which is the shape this lesson names. Answered by measurement rather than by reading: checked out the pre-fix journey.test.ts into the tree and ran it against post-fix source -- 6 failed of 16, and the six that failed are exactly the six that were rewritten. Every rewrite was forced, none was comfort, and each preserved its own subject (the fixture widened or walked out; the one changed expectation, gated.shallows dropping off the offer list, is the fix's own subject and now has a dedicated test). (2) The c9 surfaces are tested as pure builders and as a registry with fake surfaces registered inside the test; nothing asserts the real components register. Two mutants deleting the useTestSurface calls at App.tsx:45 and MapPane.tsx:127 SURVIVED the whole 2498-test suite, because the suite has no DOM environment and renders through renderToStaticMarkup, so useEffect never runs. That is a test that cannot fail while the code is present, and it is the whole of the sentence pass 5 graded unmet.

head: 13374c4d97573c9f2d348a6443ac81641cb87d14
note: gui-rebuild pass 6: the pass-5 finding named one reproduction -- a walk-away offer whose destination is undiscovered has no bubble anywhere. The fix closes that. Two neighbours found by asking what the property is rather than what the finding said. (1) A walk-away offer whose destination IS discovered but sits on another z-plane is still withdrawn from the sheet and has no bubble on the plane the player is standing on: measured live at guide-house-upstairs, where 'Travel to Basement' at legs 2 is withdrawn and surfaces.map.places on plane 1 holds two places, neither of them the basement, until map.plane -1. Filed. (2) c9's already-filed record names journey as the one published field TestState cannot read; the property is every field the shell draws, and c9's own commit made four Character subpages reachable by an agent while inventory, equipment, xp, stats, flags and encounter all stayed unreadable. Filed as its own record rather than as a recurrence, because fixing the journey one would not fix these.

head: 13374c4d97573c9f2d348a6443ac81641cb87d14
note: gui-rebuild pass 6: asked it of the new code rather than treating none-found as real. Four guesses found, three of them stated where they live and one not. Stated: useTestSurface re-reads its surface through a ref on every render because an action called a minute later must move the component as it stands now (testSurface.ts:19); zoomFrom clamps where planeFrom refuses, because the pinch it stands in for is clamped too (discovery.ts:224); walkTo returns a refusal only when no route existed at all, because a walk that crossed a leg and then found the way on shut did move the world (runtime.ts:744, and TRAPDOOR is the fixture for it). Not stated, and it is a real one the audit had to derive: routeTo may end at an undiscovered place while reachable now refuses to name one, and whether that asymmetry is reachable depends on facts in two other files -- spreadDiscovery discovering exactly the passable neighbours of the room the player arrives in, and beginAction refusing a choiceId that is not in computeChoices. Both hold today, so the asymmetry is unreachable from the shell, but nothing states that and no test asserts it as a pair.

head: 13374c4d97573c9f2d348a6443ac81641cb87d14
note: gui-rebuild pass 6: guarded it on the two new guards. The discovery gate at journey.ts:86 is the narrowing this pass exists to check, and it is not over-strict: it excludes a place from the OFFER list only, leaves locationChoices' next-door offers untouched, and every place it excludes is one the map draws no bubble for -- verified over shipped content by walking every location reachable from a fresh session and finding no choice whose leadsTo is outside status.discovered, and verified in the negative by the CHAIN and GATED fixtures. The new refusals in nav.ts and discovery.ts refuse an agent by name and clamp a zoom, which is the right split: a name nothing answers to is a mistake to report, a zoom past the stop is a legal gesture. The one over-strictness in the tree is pass 5's own filed record gui-rebuild-pass5-the-phone-sweep-refuses-every-keyboard-han, still open and untouched by this range.

head: 13374c4d97573c9f2d348a6443ac81641cb87d14
note: gui-rebuild pass 6: c9 is the clause that had failed and it is the one this applies to. Rather than hunting a second missing registration, I asked whether the clause's wording is the thing that is wrong, and half of it is. 'Actions registered by the components that own them' is a good rule and the branch met it honestly -- the registry starts empty, both components register their own state through their own closures, and unmount drops the entry. 'A production build contains no trace of it' is the half that is wrong as written: it is an absolute no ordinary module boundary can satisfy, and the branch's guard makes it look satisfied by enumerating three names. Filed against the clause with a stated boundary -- say what 'no trace' covers and read the list off its owner -- rather than as a longer list of strings to grep dist/ for.

head: 3899de976429aea19b989b40ba7d1b71a3ceb552
note: The browser agent harness does not reuse the DSL's # test system, and the two stay separate - the author ruled 2026-08-12. A # test section is a runtime directive script: its vocabulary is parsed by src/grammar, resolved by src/content and executed by applyDirective in src/runtime, and its assert: speaks about flags, inventory and counters. For a directive to say layer: map or plane: 2, grammar and runtime would have to learn shell vocabulary that src/ui owns, and since grammar < content < runtime < ui the engine would either absorb GUI concepts or call back up into src/ui, which layer-check forbids. What is reused instead is composition and pattern: src/ui/testHarness.ts may invoke runTest (src/runtime/session.ts:600) by name to set a world up, because ui imports downward from runtime for free, and a GUI script borrows /create-test's record-then-replay shape without borrowing its grammar. World state stays authored in the DSL; shell interaction stays in src/ui.

head: 3899de976429aea19b989b40ba7d1b71a3ceb552
note: Harness completeness leaves gui-rebuild and becomes its own spec - the author ruled 2026-08-12, after gui-rebuild reached ten clauses met over six audit passes. The new promise is that a driving agent needs no screenshot: it drives every interactive control and reads every field PlayStatus publishes (src/ui/testHarness.ts TestState today carries none of inventory, equipment, xp, stats, flags, encounter or journey), and it detects transient moments. The transient half is the structural one: src/ui/transient.ts is a general channel and c10 proved it, but useArrivals (src/ui/App.tsx:25) and the imperative settle transitions in src/ui/Pager.tsx and src/ui/VStack.tsx are two more transient mechanisms off it, so an animation is routed by memory today. Every transient moment is to be created through the one channel, so an unrouted animation does not play at all; and the harness must expose an accumulated log of what played since the previous step, never a snapshot, because batch() settles on setTimeout(0) and a 400ms animation begins and ends between two steps. gui-rebuild keeps only what protects what it already delivered.

note: gui-rebuild pass 7: c7 is the clause that has now carried a finding on three consecutive passes, so I asked whether its wording is what is wrong rather than hunting a fourth instance. It is, in one sentence. 'It shows one z-plane at a time, plus whatever sits off that plane and is adjacent to the player' was written as a description of a floor plan, and a28eea1 added a third category the sentence does not name: a place the view carries a walk-away offer to, drawn wherever it stands. Nothing c7 promises is missing, so this is a stated-boundary problem and not a downgrade: filed as 'amend the sentence to name what the map draws' rather than as a longer list of what the map may not draw. The precedent is e8d65f9, where the author's ruling on Edit's console went into the clause instead of into a comment.

head: cb547e7e3362fb9774baba90bad26eb6f3013b3d
note: The 2026-08-04 tool-friction-backlog ruling that docs/audits/systems.json belongs in no writes grant does not cover a task that adds NEW files to a system's paths, and every member of this branch does. cluster-shape-catalogue measured it: tasks concept refuses to register over a path the system does not already own ('a concept refines its own system and cannot reach outside it'), and no command adds a paths entry, so the manifest has to be edited by hand before the registration the ruling assumes is even possible. The ruling's subject is concurrent APPENDS through tasks concept; ownership edits are a different operation and first-class-modals already recorded taking one as grant drift. For this branch the file is granted to each member that adds a file, and the members run serially, so the collision the ruling exists to prevent cannot occur.

head: cb547e7e3362fb9774baba90bad26eb6f3013b3d
note: RULING, agreed by the author 2026-08-12: docs/audits/systems.json carries two operations and only one of them is ungrantable. Registering a concept is an append that every task makes and that no task can predict the timing of, so it stays in no write grant -- that is what the 2026-08-04 tool-friction-backlog ruling settled and it is unchanged. Declaring ownership is a different operation: a system's paths array is where file-level ownership is stated, nothing adds an entry automatically, audit-status fails on a tracked file no system owns, and tasks concept refuses to register over a path its system does not already own -- so a task that creates a file MUST edit paths, and must do it before the registration the other half of the manifest expects. That edit belongs in the creating task's write grant, whoever creates the file, so the grant says what the diff will contain. The invariant: every task that adds a tracked file grants itself docs/audits/systems.json; no task grants it in order to register a concept. Where two such tasks could run concurrently, the collision is a planner's to order, not a reason to leave the grant false. Measured by cluster-shape-catalogue on 2026-08-12, which hit the refusal directly; first-class-modals had already taken the same edit on 2026-08-09 and recorded it as grant drift, which is the same fact reported as an accident.

note: A jewel slot must be ALLOCATED before a jewel may be slotted into it. c8 and c14 name only 'blocked' and 'already filled' as slotting refusals, so this is a third the spec does not state; without it a player at level 1 can place every jewel they own, permanently and for no points, and 'a level is spent on a passive or on opening a slot alike' buys nothing but conduction. docs/smithing/cluster-jewels-draft.dsl's worked sequence allocates the e slot and then fills it, which is this order. The same sequence charges its fourth point for the FILLING step, which c13 (allocation is what points buy) and c14 (the jewel is consumed when slotted) do not support, so slotting here costs no point and the draft's four-point plan is a three-point plan plus a free slotting.

head: e812f8483ba19c12166aad2f310a3af250efdda1
note: Minting is at the first thing recorded about a copy, not specifically at the first jewel. c11 says a stack counts 'until a jewel is slotted into one', but experience is per-instance and allocation needs points, so feeding must mint too or nothing can ever be slotted -- feed, allocate and slot all mint, through the one growItem door. Feeding may overshoot the ceiling: the refusal is on the level, so the last feed below max-level is accepted whole and itemLevel caps rather than the experience being truncated; nothing reads experience except level(xp). And an item instance is never 'empty': pruneInstances DESTROYS an emptied payload rather than handing the copy back to its stack, so an honest empty() would delete a player's item when content moved under a level-1 plane.

head: e812f8483ba19c12166aad2f310a3af250efdda1
note: The plane payload stores the origin cluster's jewel id (null meaning the base's default point-with-an-east-slot) rather than deriving it from the item template, because InstanceKind.repair is handed a payload, a registry and a liveness predicate and never the template it belongs to. A cluster effect is stored as the id of the item that applied it, not as its percentage: the payload then holds no number but the experience, and an effect whose declaration is gone is repairable the way a slotted jewel is.

note: The author decided 2026-08-12 that an instance id is the carried thing: equipped may hold one, the instance table is where a modified item lives, and statRange resolves it rather than reading a stack count. The alternative considered and rejected was letting a modified item keep its stack entry, which needs no change to equip or statRange and breaks concretely on two modified copies of one base -- inventory reads 2, two instances name the same template, and nothing says which is worn. The author added a second rule: an instanced item stacks only with an exact duplicate of itself. This branch does not merge instances at all, which is the conservative reading of that rule -- it can miss a legitimate merge but can never make a wrong one -- and duplicate detection waits until content can produce two identical planes. The gap was found by cluster-plane-runtime's worker, not by the spec: c20 says an item's contribution reaches combat through the equipped path and c11 makes a modified item leave the stack, and nothing stated the half where those two meet.

note: The target of every growth verb is an item id or a minted instance id, and the load-time reference check must discriminate on shape rather than being dropped. Found by the wearing slice: an instance id is minted at runtime, so a directive naming one cannot resolve at load, and today equip: refuses it as an unknown item -- which means no # test can wear or grow a copy, and c22 needs one that does all four verbs. Exempting the argument entirely would buy that by losing the guarantee that a typo'd item id in an authored # test is caught at load, which is the whole value of the site. The invariant to hold: a target that cannot possibly be a minted id is still resolved at load, and one that could be is deferred to the runtime, which already refuses an id naming no live instance. Minting is deterministic -- it draws no randomness and no clock, and the counter never rewinds -- so an authored test can name a copy it just made. Decide the spelling once for all five verbs; do not solve it per verb.

head: dded918d760f260d310930c14cc6c0b98fbe820b
note: The same cluster-effect item cannot be applied twice to one cluster: recordEffect refuses the repeat. isCluster in clusterPlane.ts already validates a cluster's effects with hasNoRepeats, shipped by cluster-plane-runtime, so recording a second copy would mint a plane that isPlane rejects and loadSave throws on -- the effect would survive until the player reloaded and then take the whole instance with it. Two stacking effects are therefore two declarations, which c17's worked case reads as naturally ('one 25% effect' then 'a second'). If content wants one orb the player can use twice on a cluster, the substrate has to change effects from a set to a list first, and c15's mod-slots capacity is what would bound it.

head: dded918d760f260d310930c14cc6c0b98fbe820b
note: A cluster's mod-slots capacity is read off the jewel standing in the hex, through placementAt, not off the item that owns the plane. So a cluster from a jewel declaring mod-slots: 1 takes one effect, and the base cluster an item carries when it declares no cluster-jewel: takes DEFAULT_MOD_SLOTS -- BASE_CLUSTER already sets that field, so a plain item's origin hex is moddable rather than a special case. The spec says 'its mod-slots: capacity' without saying whose, and the jewel is the only reading under which two different jewels in one plane can differ.

note: The four growth verbs are spelled one per runtime function, not one verb dispatching on what the consumed item declares: 'feed: <target> with <item>', 'slot: <target> at <q>,<r> <direction> with <jewel>', 'allocate: <target> at <q>,<r> position <n>' or '... slot <direction>', 'apply: <target> at <q>,<r> with <effect>'. Allocation consumes nothing and the three that do consume take different addresses, so a single verb would have had to decide after parsing which of its arguments were required, which is a rule in the router. A hex is spelled the way a plane keys one and read back through parseHexKey, so a non-canonical address fails at parse. The # test regression c22 writes is written against these.

head: fd294fe1d35056136276fdd05785c14a22b92916
note: 'refuse: <growth verb> <payload>' is a fifth directive kind, added because c22 has to record each refusal in a # test that replays green and c14 asks for a checked outcome rather than an absence: without it a refused verb aborts the replay and the only alternative -- attempting it and asserting the consumed item is intact -- passes for the wrong reason when the target is typo'd. It is scoped to the four growth verbs because their refusal is a value growItem returns; every other verb pushes a sentence into the log and leaves nothing to invert. Note the consequence: a 'refuse:' whose growth the plane allowed fails the test with the world already moved, since there is no way to know it succeeded without doing it. The CLI records 'refuse:' when a typed verb was turned down, so a test authored from live play asserts the session it was taken from.

note: RULING, by the author 2026-08-12: a modal prefills a directive's leading arguments and never narrows the grammar. The invariant, not the instance: every growth directive stays spellable in full from anywhere the directive surface is reachable, and a screen's short form is the same directive kind with arguments defaulted from its frame -- one parser, never two spellings that can drift. The reason is forward-looking rather than aesthetic: a short form defined as its own thing bakes in the assumption that a screen shows exactly one hexagon of exactly one item, and a screen that later shows a whole tree, or two items side by side, would have to break its own grammar to address the second one. head: 239c0e4dd91f510ed69c3f31f46064b6cd0d7df9
note: items-mods-and-crafting pass 1, on c15. The clause is four sentences and three of them are proved: the effect is consumed and recorded against the cluster it was used on, the orb stays a stack, and the mod-slots capacity refusal holds with the item intact (mutation-tested, KILLED). The fourth - 'never to a jewel in inventory' - fails outright: applyClusterEffect hands its target to growItem, which accepts any item id, so a stacked cluster jewel de-stacks into an instance and takes the effect. Passes 1 and 2 both mutation-tested extensively and named their verdicts in the spec's prose - pass 1 names nine mutations, pass 2 names another six, including three separate ways of neutering the not-a-base refusal - and NOT ONE of them was re-runnable, because no manifest of theirs survives on the shared temp path. Only their pass files do (audit-items-mods-and-crafting-pass1.txt and -pass2.txt are still there; no mutations.json is). So I reconstructed the c9 root-position and origin-root mutations from pass 2's English, which is the third pass paying for the second pass's work a second time. My own two manifests are in a session scratchpad and will be gone before pass 4, so the same bill lands again. tasks audit accepting the manifest it just told me to build - and audit-prompt reprinting the previous pass's - is what converts a paragraph naming a mutation into a command a later pass can run.

note: combat-events pass 4, and this is the second-branch case the record's own deliverable names, on a different spec. combat-events was decomposed into combat-hook-grammar (merged, audited at 6757444) and combat-hook-firing; this branch is the second one. git merge-base --is-ancestor 6757444 3b35539 succeeds only because the FIRST branch's pass head merged and this branch was then cut from a later main, so slugStanding set lastPassMerged and the brief printed 'combat-events merged before this branch began, so none of the work its clauses describe is in the diff above', wrote no pass file, wrote no mutation manifest, and made step 7 'Do not file a pass'. Every part of that is false and the store says so in three places the tool did not read: combat-hook-firing is a member carrying spec: combat-events, discharges c2 c5 c6 c7 c8 c9 c10 c11, and was closed by 125f230 inside this very range; tasks spec show combat-events reported five clauses outstanding; and merge-ready's own spec leg passed with 'every member of combat-events this branch declared is closed' in the same invocation whose clauses leg failed on those five. Cost: the brief handed me nothing for steps 4 and 7, so the 14-entry manifest that produced this pass's whole result (12 killed, 2 survived, both survivors became findings) was built by hand from cold reads of runtime.ts, stats.ts, effects.ts and hooks.ts, about 30 minutes; and I had to decide against the brief's own step 7 to file at all. The counterfactual is measurable this time: had I obeyed step 7, six clauses -- c2, c6, c7, c8, c9 and c10, i.e. the entire runtime half of the spec, unknown or unmet since pass 1 -- would have stayed outstanding with the implementation that discharges them sitting green in the diff, and the branch would have been unmergeable on its clauses leg forever. Also worth the record: pass 1's and pass 3's manifests are still on the shared temp path but both aim at src/grammar and src/content, so nothing could be carried forward into the runtime slice.

note: combat-events pass 4 merge gate. npm run tasks -- merge-ready reported 'npm test FAIL exit=1' as one of its legs and named no test, so the leg says only that something went red. Re-running the identical command it prints as the repro, npm test -- --reporter=dot, in the same worktree with nothing changed, passed whole: 115 test files, 2732 tests, 0 failed, 32s. So the gate's own verdict and a direct re-run of the gate's own command disagree on an unmodified tree, and an auditor cannot tell a flake from a real failure without paying the five minutes twice. Compounding it: merge-ready's leg prints no failure names at all, where mutate's tallyOf refuses a run it cannot attribute to a named test -- the same repo already has the discipline that would have made this one line instead of a second full suite run. Cost about 6 minutes and one moment of believing the branch was red.

note: DECISION (plane-frame): the plane screen publishes feed: alongside slot: and allocate:, which the deliverable's enumeration of options did not include. Measured: a base still in its stack is level 1 with exactly one point (skillLevel(0) is 1), so a screen offering only slot and allocate spends that point and is a dead end forever - experience is the only thing that buys another and no other surface in this branch offers it, so the author would still have to type feed: to play the feature this spec exists to make playable. It also makes the per-verb prefill c4 asks for real rather than one hardcoded prefix: feed: fills in the copy and not the hexagon, slot: and allocate: fill in both, which is what onCopy and onHexagon in planeScreen.ts are. c13's route does not walk feed and does not have to.

head: 57817af02a14faef893a0508c97b33ac9128a012
note: c21 needed a fourth reader corrected and a distinction the clause did not name. The spec recorded stats.ts as unaffected because what an equipped item contributes is read off state.equipped; it is, but each worn id was then guarded on carriesItem, which under c21 is false for everything worn, so the fold would have contributed nothing at all. Guard removed. The distinction: a worn copy is out of the stack, so every reader asking 'does the player carry this' would have had wearing your only blade revoke the requires: has gate, the recipe, the item action and the cost that name it - the same defect class the 2026-08-13 regression audit filed against growing, now caused by wearing, and reproduced live by carriedItem.test.ts. So the one read publishes three places rather than two and the two questions are named apart: carriedCount is what an inventory row states (a stack of three with one worn reads two, which is c21's own sentence), heldCount is what a gate asks (having a thing and carrying it are two questions, and only one of them is the stack). Growing what you wear needed no grammar change: wearInstead's rule - the slot follows the copy that left the stack - becomes the source a mint comes out of, the stack while it has one and the slot once it has not, which is the same rule evaluated before the take instead of after. Destroy reads the same rule, so destroying what you wear empties the slot rather than reaching into a stack that is not where the copy is. Judgement on fixtures: no shipped # save carries an equipped slot, so content needs no migration; carriedItem.test.ts's one-blade held the blade carried and worn at once, which under c21 spells two blades and is not what any test on it is about, so it was re-recorded as the one blade worn. The modal lists both sides in one screen and the entry names the slot it is worn in, which is what lets the equipment's rows offer the verbs a carried row does; c21's 'listed under equipment and nowhere else' is kept at the page level, where the GUI's two pages filter on that field.

head: 57817af02a14faef893a0508c97b33ac9128a012
note: What c21 leaves for this member. PlayStatus.carried now holds both sides of the partition, one row per copy, and a worn row carries a slot field that a carried row does not - so the Character layer's two pages are one filter on that field and neither needs a second record. src/ui/sheet.ts already does the carried half (carried() drops the rows with a slot, worn() is unchanged and resolves its names out of those same rows). What is left is the acting half: App.tsx draws the equipment page as a Ledger with no onOpen, so the worn rows are the only rows on either page that cannot be pressed, and the verbs the runtime now offers them - Grow, Unequip, Destroy - are unreachable from the GUI. A worn row's published value is 'Name (slot)', which is what /inv <value> takes, so it is the same dispatch a carried row already makes.

The property behind pass 1's finding is 'one copy, one id, and every route reaches the copy the row is of', and the storage underneath still violates it: state.equipped holds the bare item id for a worn stack copy, so wornIn(state,'iron-sword') is still true of the stack, and carriesItem -- the one reader 486e15c did not teach the new spelling -- returns false for a stack of two because one is worn. The same throw fires with a stack of three and is then plainly wrong, and nothing in the file distinguishes the two. Asked the lesson's question of the fix commit's own new tests too and they answer: 486e15c's commit message says the three tests the pass 1 audit named as misleading left the stack at zero so stackCopy fell through to the slot and reached the right copy by accident, and all three now keep a stack standing behind the slot -- I re-read them and that is what they do. All three are real choices and all three are stated. One guess is NOT stated and I filed it low: named() falls back to the spelling itself when the slot is empty (state.equipped[slot] ?? id), which turns an internal id into an item name, and two player-facing sentences then print it -- '/inv worn:offhand' answers 'you carry no worn:offhand' and planeStale says 'it grows worn:mainhand'. head: 540fbfaa8cf1cd214d604569b6eb013356ffe348
note: crafting-modal pass 2: guarded the new guard both ways and the over-strict end is where this pass's HIGH finding lives, which is the lesson firing rather than passing. carriesItem's new early return 'if (wornIn(state,id) !== undefined) return false' is a narrowing added by this branch's c21 work, and it over-refuses: it is meant to say 'this worn copy is not on the carried side' and it says 'no copy of this item is on the carried side', so equip() refuses legitimate input -- a second copy off a stack of three, and an authored 'equip: <item>' directive. Also checked the other new refusals for over-reach and they are right: command.ts's '/inventory lets a slot spelling through unresolved' widens rather than narrows, planeReport's targeted() replaced two conditions with hasStackCopy and admits exactly the same set plus the slot spelling, and carriedScreen's Equip/Unequip applies-filters are complementary on entry.slot so no entry can lose both.

It is not: 'an entry offers only verbs that apply to it' is the right rule, and what is wrong is that the branch has now enumerated the readers of one word twice and got the list wrong both times. c21's own text records the first correction (it claimed the equipped-contribution fold was unaffected and it was not), and 486e15c is the second (it taught five id-taking functions the worn-copy spelling and missed carriesItem). I also checked the one place two clauses of this spec could contradict each other -- c1's enumeration says Equip applies to 'an item with a slot', which the carried stack row satisfies, while c18's gloss says a verb offered must not be one that does nothing -- and graded them differently on that stated boundary rather than resolving it silently: c1 met on its own enumeration, c18 unmet on its gloss, said in both evidence blocks.

note: reimplement-localization pass 1, the sentinel-expansion half: audit-prompt wrote 155 entries for nine clauses, every one a sentinel, expanded per test in the file the clause's proof line names. Because four clauses (c2/c4 and c6/c7/c8) share two test files, the same eleven and fourteen tests were emitted three and four times under different clause prefixes; c3 got 56 entries, i.e. every test in session.test.ts including the whole pre-existing journey, modal and growth suite. c1 and c9 got zero, their proof targets being npx tsc --noEmit and npm test, which resolve to no named test. All 155 discarded; a 14-entry manifest hand-built against the lines the clauses are actually about, 11 killed and 3 survived, roughly 25 minutes. The three survivors are the whole pass and none is reachable by a per-test expansion: itemExamine's English-article guard (a line whose own named test asserts a value the guard cannot change), EngineKey's literal union (a type, invisible to vitest at every scope), and mergePass's locale skip (a line nothing depends on). The generated file's only contribution was again the derived test titles.

note: buffs-generalized pass 1: asked it of every assertion in the new 286-line buffs.test.ts, and the answer is that they can all fail - my own 10-entry manifest, aimed at lines I picked rather than the implementer's, came back 10 KILLED with each verdict naming a distinct test. The one shape that could have hidden is c6: 'pays five stacks of +6 attack out as +30' would still pass if the fold multiplied by a count instead of reading five carriers, so I mutated modifierCarriers to push one carrier per source id rather than mutating any arithmetic, and it died there. Same question of c7's 17.6/26.4 case: the expectation is arithmetic on the authored numbers, not derived from the structure under test.

head: 07fa1e9129159d79c02dd3fdeef8a3bccc7fc87c
note: buffs-generalized pass 1: the branch's own reproduction is 'save.ts parses a key string apart', and the property behind it is 'nobody outside the module knows what a buff is made of'. Hunted the neighbour rather than the fix: found that pruneBuffs still hard-codes registry.items.has(buff.source), so the module that was made the single owner of a buff's identity has quietly made every non-item source unloadable, with a warning naming a cause that is false - filed medium. Second neighbour, same property: isTagClause hand-copies the three TagClause kinds, so the module owning what a buff is made of keeps a second, unchecked copy of the grammar's union - filed low.

head: 07fa1e9129159d79c02dd3fdeef8a3bccc7fc87c
note: buffs-generalized pass 1: guarded both ends of the new save guard. Too loose: isBuffList admits a stat-bonus tag carrying no amount, which loads with no warning and then throws a raw TypeError out of statRange - filed medium, reproduced through npm run inspect. Too strict: the same predicate hard-codes the three TagClause kinds, so a fourth kind would make it refuse legitimate saves with nothing at compile time to say so - filed low. Also checked pruneBuffs' new holder rule for over-reach and it is right: actorLoaded is supplied by save.ts, which is where who counts as a character is already decided, and my mutation replacing it with () => true was killed.

head: 07fa1e9129159d79c02dd3fdeef8a3bccc7fc87c
note: buffs-generalized pass 1: asked it rather than reporting none found, and two guesses are unstated. First, whether a source stacks is read off an unvalidated free-form keyword - grammar/tagClause.ts accepts any bare word as a keyword and no registry of known keywords exists anywhere - so 'stacking' or 'stack' silently selects replace, with no diagnostic at any layer; filed low. Second, pruneBuffs guesses that every buff source is a registered # item while BuffSource is deliberately typed {id, tags}; the guess is pinned as correct by buffs.test.ts:271 rather than stated; filed medium. The guesses that ARE stated and defensible: the fight-scoped clear in endAction, and the readonly-plus-cast ownership pattern, which copies effects.ts:317 and modals.ts:127.

head: 07fa1e9129159d79c02dd3fdeef8a3bccc7fc87c

The rule that makes it fail is save.ts:13, 'with no migration path, a stale save is rejected', which is the repository's standing policy and not this branch's; the honest result is the stated boundary rather than a finding against this branch, so c9 is deferred with the policy and the owning save-migration-system task named in the evidence, which is what converts it into a tracked undelivered record.

note: reimplement-localization pass 6, and it is the flag-SHAPE half a second time on this spec, exactly as the 2026-08-09 full-refactor-of-enemies-and-combat pass 2 occurrence describes. The generated pass file writes every clause flag as --proof N= and --evidence N=, and its commented finding block is '# --finding ' with a trailing space, so the two families use different shapes with nothing saying so. Writing the four finding blocks as --finding=<title> refused the whole file with 'error: --finding=A describes a finding, and no --finding has been opened yet' — a message that names as unopened the very flag it is complaining about, and names no line and no file. Cost one refused filing and a scripted rewrite of seven flag names across four blocks. note: what-is-stored-or-replayed-is-an-id pass 2: paid it, and the reason is worth recording because it is not carelessness. I re-ran the identical command with 'head' to read the confirmation I had just been denied, and that second run filed a second pass and a second copy of all three findings with no warning that the same base..head and the same clause set had already been recorded. note: A recorded modal answer is a protocol, not a TypeScript constant, and stays the value rather than becoming an index. The 2026-08-14 decision on content/engine-en.dsl was right in substance and wrong in wording: every submit-modal: the shipped content records is a content id (race=elf, item=tutorial-island.iron-sword), an engine verb (verb=grow), a directive tail (plane=allocate: slot e) or typed free text (name=Rowan) - none of it English a translator would touch. Recording the index instead was raised by the author and is refused on two measurements: ModalOption.values is null for free text so there is no list to index, and an item id indexes a list whose order depends on what the player picked up, so a recorded index selects a different object once the list moves while the recording still passes. Both drivers continue to answer by index and convert to the value at command.ts:492, which is crafting-modal's ruling and a different question.

head: 3565906fc41f1e4709de4bf605bf641affcf99ec
note: c6 key scheme, decided where the spec was silent: a say: result is <ns>.<kind>.<id>.say.<n> under the section that AUTHORED it, and a dialogue's lines hang under the node - <node>.line.<n>, .choice.<n>, .again, and .say.<n> for a say: result inside a node or a choice. Owner is the authoring section rather than the action, because a hook, a handler block and a droptable have no address of their own and inventing one would collide with c7's action-address work; keying off the section also means an action an entity uses: is keyed once, under its declaration, which is c7's property arrived at from the other side.

head: 3565906fc41f1e4709de4bf605bf641affcf99ec
note: c6: Localizer.prose retires, and with it Locales.moduleLanguages and engine.text.untranslated. Every line that went through the prose door is addressed now, so nothing genuinely unkeyable is left: a say: with no key can only be a result built in code, and there is no language it could be shown in, so it is a RuntimeError rather than a marker. A player of an untranslated language reads the key, which is what every other door already answers with (c3).

head: 3565906fc41f1e4709de4bf605bf641affcf99ec
note: c6: two prose doors rather than one. spoken(key) prints a say: as written, because its braces are the author's own punctuation and routing it through the segment grammar would give it interpolation the DSL does not have today. line(key, render) reads a dialogue line back through the segment grammar it was authored in. The render is passed in rather than done inside the localizer because localized.ts importing conditions.ts closes a cycle through itemInstance.ts's module-level defineInstanceKind, measured by four test files failing to collect.

head: e1a2d7c1ba133896ff55122d48515bef6d8e7647
note: c10: /state is not a driver drawing to a player. Its dictionaries are keyed by the ids the engine stores under and answer to whoever is driving the session, so they are ToolLines and the walk never sees them - the exemption is the words: 'tool' discriminant c4 already declares and published.test.ts already stops at, not a list of strings. The same ruling covers the modal banner and the free-text prompt, which spell a screen's id and the keys a submit-modal: answers it by. The pools under /state stay PlayerLines: they are the same words a player reads anywhere else. The cost is that the tool channel can now carry invented English nobody walks, which is c4's boundary and not new here.

head: e1a2d7c1ba133896ff55122d48515bef6d8e7647
note: c10's enforcement over the REPL is a two-language diff, not a permission list: the same script is played in the base language and in translationOf() of the same universe, and every run of letters that survives the change of language is a word no locale produced. Four things may leave one standing, each derived rather than named - a bearing from DIRECTIONS (a coordinate spelled with letters, sitting beside 1,0 in the same report); a token the engine spelled into words it published itself (the e inside 'allocate: slot e'); the player's own typed line quoted back; and c10's own sentence, an id drawn where the row's published words are drawn too. Which of a published field's values are ids and which are words is read off the two renderings rather than from a type, so a field added tomorrow is classified by the engine's own behaviour. The walk lives at scripts/printedWords.test.ts because scripts sits above runtime and may import both drivers, which src/runtime cannot.

head: e1a2d7c1ba133896ff55122d48515bef6d8e7647
note: The brand walk and the engine-sentence walk moved out of src/runtime/localized.test.ts and now enumerate shippedModules() - sweptFiles(trackedFiles()) minus tests, the same enumeration layer-check sweeps. They walked sourceFiles('src') and so reached one of the two drivers; an 'as Localized' cast and a whole engine sentence in scripts/ both survived 3094 tests. They had to move rather than widen because src/runtime importing scripts/lib/layers.ts reaches up a layer, and a second copy of SOURCE_TREES is the manual-sync failure CLAUDE.md forbids.

note: archetype-mods pass 1: audit-prompt wrote 298 sentinel entries for twelve clauses - every clause crossed with every test in each file its proof line names, so c1 alone opened with the eleven passive.test.ts titles beside itemContribution.test.ts's and integration.test.ts's, and c3/c4/c6 repeated integration.test.ts's block three times over. head: fd84e5ee280ab0f1f1de0795ae1aaaa357ef881e
note: archetype-mods pass 1: one failed filing, same prefix-classification defect and the same message. My clause-11 evidence quotes probe's own flag, and the sentence wrapped so that the line began with the token; the refusal read '--round-trip describes a finding, and no --finding has been opened yet' and named neither the line number nor the file, so the offender was found by grepping the pass file for ^-- and diffing that against the flag set - the identical recovery the 2026-08-08 orchestrator occurrence describes, run again unchanged. The token here is not even a tasks flag: any '--word' at column zero is classified as one, so an auditor quoting probe, vitest, npm or git in its evidence pays this. What would end it is either classifying only against the known flag set for the subcommand, or naming the line in the refusal so the fix is one edit rather than a grep.

note: The playbot is ONE loop with two prompts, ruled by the author 2026-08-15, and exploratory-playbot's requires edge on starting-zone inverts. Filling a half-built world and hunting bugs in a finished one are the same turn: show a view, pick a choiceId, report what you tried and could not do. head: bcdc68b3fc606fe2afabffefef3e1cc204488a59
note: The playbot runs on the Claude Agent SDK, not the Messages API: the author ruled 2026-08-15 that it must be startable from Claude Code because that is where the subscription is. Agent SDK usage and claude -p draw on the plan's usage limits (the separate Agent SDK credit announced for 2026-06-15 was paused), while an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY bills a Platform account pay-as-you-go and would put a long authoring session in the wrong pocket. Plan auth covers ordinary individual use; a product other people run needs a key, and that is the line this revisits if it is ever crossed. Adds c4, the harness floor: the SDK is Claude Code packaged as a library and loads its own system prompt, its tools and this repo's CLAUDE.md by default, all of which must be off. No other clause moved, because c2 made the model a parameter.

head: b4e0fc51eb2136e94fc5fe5ab915c34d680bf566
note: c6 narrows to what the engine can honour, ruled by the author 2026-08-15. A twelve-turn spike found a turn has two input surfaces, not one -- a choice takes apply(session, choiceId) and an open screen takes an applyDirective submit-modal -- and that the engine is inconsistent about selector stability: a choice id and a character-creation value are names that survive an edit, while a dialogue option's value is its index. The original promise, that a reordering list cannot change what a reply selects, was therefore false on exactly the surface an author edits most. The clause now promises only that the loop introduces no positional coupling of its own; the residue is a known engine property, out of scope for this branch, and wants its own record if it is ever fixed.

note: The playbot's ordering edge on starting-zone is restored, ruled by the author 2026-08-15. It was dropped on the premise that the loop is the authoring rig and the zone its output; a spike the same day found the premise only half true. The expected field is real authoring output on a half-built world, but a player cannot walk to the edge of a world with no rooms, so the loop cannot bootstrap a zone from nothing. With that gone the original edge is right. Also ruled out: the loop must not author the world it plays, because an agent cannot be surprised by its own room and expected collapses, which is c9 read from the other end; and 'an agent prompts me and I GM' is a presentation over the same log, not a second architecture -- it is a second system prompt, the slot c1 already reserves.

note: The local file is the one source of truth and localSource.text is a cache of the last adopt, so every command composes its next text from localChangesNow. /local clear is the one exception and needs none: it renders a fresh header from dependencies and reads nothing. A count of localSource.text reads in command.ts is what states the rule for commands not written yet, because a behaviour test can only speak for the sites that exist.

head: 8ed8623bee67edceb9b00e1f125f932ede8a17bc
note: a-session-adopts-an-edit-or-refuses-it-whole pass 2, occurrence 42: audit-prompt generated 585 sentinel entries for six clauses over one spec whose clauses DO carry proof: vitest lines - so this is the sentinel-expansion half at its worst, one entry per test in each named file, 585 of them, none aimed. All 585 discarded and a 16-entry manifest hand-built at audit-...-pass2-mutations.json. 14 killed, 2 survived, and both survivors are the pass's two medium findings. Neither is reachable by a per-test expansion: one is the second disjunct of a gate inside a function no test names, and the other is src/runtime/session.ts:387, a line in a file NO clause's proof line mentions for c5 at all - c5's proof is 'vitest src/runtime/command.test.ts', so every one of the generator's c5 entries would have been aimed at a test in command.test.ts while the line that decides c5's log half lives in session.ts. Aiming cost about 20 minutes and is again the entire result. What I could carry forward: pass 1's own hand-aimed manifests were still on the shared temp path and named in the spec's prose, which is the only reason I could re-run its five entries at this head before writing my own.

head: 8ed8623bee67edceb9b00e1f125f932ede8a17bc
note: a-session-adopts-an-edit-or-refuses-it-whole pass 2: paid the setup, dodged the charge, and the dodge is the reportable part. tasks audit --args-from succeeded and my invocation was piped to tail -40, which showed only the prior-art dump and the rulings block - the confirmation line, the finding count and the Next: line were all above the cut, exactly as the two prior occurrences describe. The re-run with head is the trap, and the only reason I did not take it is that I had read this record's two occurrences beforehand and reached for 'tasks show <slug>' instead, which errored with 'matches 7 ids' and thereby listed the four new pass2- finding ids - i.e. I confirmed the write through an error message from an unrelated command. So the record's cost is not only the duplicate passes it has already caused; it is that verifying a write requires knowing folklore that is not printed anywhere in the tool's own output. Printing the verdict last, or gating a second pass at the same head behind --force, still fixes it.

head: 8ed8623bee67edceb9b00e1f125f932ede8a17bc
note: a-session-adopts-an-edit-or-refuses-it-whole pass 2, and the lesson paid twice on one branch. Pass 1's medium was 'every command rewrites the whole local file from the remembered copy'; the fix took the body sections from the file and left the # info header composed from authoring.dependencies, so 'required extra' declared by the other process is still silently dropped by the next /dsl - filed medium, measured through the real command path. Second neighbour, different axis: instead of re-running pass 1's five mutants I aimed at lines pass 1 never broke, and the one that mattered - session.ts:387's log cursor - is in a file c5's proof line does not name at all. It survived the whole suite; filed medium. Both are exactly the predicted shape, a fix aimed at the finding's text rather than at the property.

head: 8ed8623bee67edceb9b00e1f125f932ede8a17bc
note: a-session-adopts-an-edit-or-refuses-it-whole pass 2: asked it of every clause and one answered badly. c5 promises 'same registry contents, same state, same log length, same clock' and its test asserts expect(first.view?.said).toEqual([]) - which cannot be false, because the fixture's session has nothing undrained in state.log at the moment it reloads (measured 0 via npm run inspect), and snapshotOf covers neither log nor cursor since serializeSession is the 17 SAVE_FIELDS and sessionStatus is location/entities/time. Confirmed by mutation: session.ts:387 logCursor -> 0 SURVIVED the whole 3272-test suite. Filed medium. The two structural tests this branch added pass the same question honestly: both derive their subjects by scanning src/runtime/command.ts rather than enumerating call sites, and I killed both from the other direction by adding a second read of localSource.text rather than by removing one.

head: 8ed8623bee67edceb9b00e1f125f932ede8a17bc
note: a-session-adopts-an-edit-or-refuses-it-whole pass 2: guarded both ends of the adopt gate, and over-strictness is where the branch actually costs something. Too loose: eleven-plus hostile local-file texts through loadUniverseWithDiagnostics (empty, no # info header, a foreign module id, a redeclaration of a base module, an unresolvable requires, NUL/control bytes, a bad field, header only) - none escapes into the session, and the gate's first disjunct always fires before the second, so I found no input that reaches localStatus?.loaded !== true and reported it as a defensive disjunct rather than as a hole. Too strict: an unparseable file another process left on disk now refuses /dsl, /local list AND /local delete with a bare DSL error identical to the one a player gets for their own typo, and only /local clear - which destroys that file - still works. Filed low: refusing is the right trade, saying whose text failed is what is missing.

head: 8ed8623bee67edceb9b00e1f125f932ede8a17bc
note: a-session-adopts-an-edit-or-refuses-it-whole pass 2: asked it rather than reporting none found, and one guess is unstated and wrong. runSectionEdit and runLocal delete pass authoring.dependencies - the module list this process loaded at startup - into upsertLocalSection/deleteLocalSection, which rebuild the whole # info block from it. That is a guess that the file's dependency header is this session's dependency header, and it is silently false the moment two processes load different content; measured, 'required extra' vanishes with no word said. Filed medium. Two other guesses were checked and are fine because they are stated: localChangesNow's fallback to localSource.text when no reader exists is written down and tested ('refuses when the context has no reader'), and /local clear's deliberate refusal to read is stated at its case label and is the 2026-08-16 ruling's own exception.

head: 8ed8623bee67edceb9b00e1f125f932ede8a17bc
note: a-session-adopts-an-edit-or-refuses-it-whole pass 2: the trigger did not fire - no clause has failed twice, pass 1 graded all six met - but I asked it of the one clause I graded unmet. c6's rule is that npm run tasks -- merge-ready passes, and it fails only on the base leg because main advanced 24 commits with the xp-from-events merge after this branch was cut. Asked whether the rule is wrong, i.e. whether an auditor should read past a base failure the diff did not cause: no. The gate's whole job is that the branch is green against the main it will land on, git merge-tree shows the merge is conflict-free but the two sides both touch src/runtime and src/content/registry.ts, and nothing has run the suite over the merged tree. Grading met would have recorded that the gate passes when the tool prints NOT merge-ready. The stated boundary is in the evidence: seven legs pass, one fails, the repair is 'git merge main' and re-run.
